                                      PROJECT NO. 58481


     RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                      §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
     LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                   §
     STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561               §
                                                                        OF TEXAS

                    TRAMMELL CROW COMPANY’S COMMENTS
                 ON PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF 16 TAC § 25.194


I.       INTRODUCTION

         Trammell Crow Company ("TCC") respectfully submits the following comments on

 proposed 16 Tex. Admin. Code ("TAC") § 25.194 implementing Public Utility Regulatory Act

 ("PURA") § 37.0561 regarding interconnection standards for large load customers in the ERCOT

 region. As a developer of large-scale data center infrastructure in Texas, TCC is committed to

 supporting a reliable, efficient, and transparent interconnection framework that enables continued

 economic growth while maintaining system integrity.

         TCC supports the Commission's objective of establishing interconnection standards that

 are designed to support business development in this state while minimizing the potential for

 stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability, as mandated by PURA § 37.0561.

 The transition to a coordinated batch study process represents a meaningful and constructive step

 toward improving planning efficiency and managing the unprecedented volume of large load

 interconnection requests in ERCOT. TCC appreciates the work of Commission Staff in developing

 the Proposal for Publication and the opportunity to offer constructive feedback.

         While TCC supports the overall direction of the proposed rule, targeted refinements to the

 financial security and refund framework are necessary to ensure that the rule achieves its statutory

 objectives without imposing financial consequences that are disproportionate to actual system


                                                  1
 costs, disconnected from cost-causation principles, and ultimately counterproductive to the

business development goals that PURA § 37.0561 is intended to advance.

       In particular, the proposed financial security requirement of $50,000 per MW at the

intermediate agreement stage, coupled with the largely non-refundable character of that security

upon withdrawal, creates a framework that fundamentally misaligns the economic incentives of

developers and interconnecting utilities. Rather than functioning as a cost-recovery mechanism

proportionate to actual utility exposure, the proposed structure creates the opportunity for utilities

to benefit financially from developer attrition—retaining substantial sums that bear no relationship

to costs actually incurred. This result is not grounded in cost-causation principles and is at odds

with the legislative mandate of PURA § 37.0561 to support business development.

       The proposed rule’s cumulative financial exposure also raises significant competitive

concerns. Under the proposed rule, only the largest and most heavily capitalized entities—such as

hyperscale data center operators with extensive balance sheets—can reasonably absorb the risk of

forfeiting up to 80% of multi-million dollar financial security postings. Smaller and mid-market

developers, including those in manufacturing, industrial, and diversified real estate development,

face disproportionate risk that may effectively preclude their participation in the ERCOT

interconnection process. This dynamic will concentrate market participation among a small

number of dominant firms, limit competition in the large-load sector, and risk creating larger

monopolies in the data center market—an outcome that does not serve the broader purpose of

PURA § 37.0561. The Commission’s large load interconnection framework should promote a

diverse and competitive market for large-load development in Texas, not inadvertently erect

financial barriers that consolidate market power.




                                                  2
        To better align the financial security framework with cost-causation principles and the

progression of the interconnection process, TCC recommends that the Commission adopt a tiered

structure, with the per-MW financial security requirement set at $25,000 per MW at the

intermediate agreement stage—where informational uncertainty is at its highest—and stepping up

to the full $50,000 per MW at the interconnection agreement stage, where the developer has the

benefit of completed study results and can make a fully informed investment commitment. This

recommendation is discussed in greater detail in Section V of these comments.

       TCC further notes that as additional large load customers come online and begin paying

for transmission service, the costs of system upgrades will be shared across a broader base of

customers, making the transmission system more affordable for all ratepayers over time. This long-

term cost-sharing dynamic underscores that the proposed forfeiture provisions overstate the actual

risk to ratepayers and to system reliability.

       Finally, TCC supports the approach reflected in Commission Staff’s memorandum filed on

April 13, 2026, recommending that rule-related interconnection requirements be separated from

ERCOT’s Planning Guide Revision Request 145 (PGRR145). Interconnection standards and

associated financial security requirements are more appropriately established through this

rulemaking proceeding, and TCC encourages the Commission to ensure that the substantive

requirements adopted in this rule are tied directly to requirements included in ERCOT’s PGRR145.

       These comments focus on four principal concerns:

                       •   the non-refundable character of financial security posted at the

                           intermediate agreement stage under proposed § 25.194(d)(10);


                       •   the 80% non-refundable forfeiture structure applicable upon withdrawal

                           or non-utilization under proposed §§ 25.194(g) and (h);

                                                3
                         •   the five-year post-energization security retention period under proposed

                            § 25.194(i); and


                        •   the timing and amount of financial security required at the intermediate

                            agreement stage, including the need for a tiered security structure and

                            an extended security posting window at the interconnection agreement

                            phase.


 TCC respectfully submits that each of these provisions, as currently structured, warrants revision.


II.     NON-REFUNDABILITY OF FINANCIAL SECURITY AT THE
        INTERMEDIATE AGREEMENT STAGE

 A.     The Proposed Structure


        Under proposed § 25.194(d)(10), a large load customer must post financial security in the

 amount of $50,000 per MW of requested peak demand at the time the intermediate agreement is

 executed. This financial security is posted before the large load customer's interconnection request

 is submitted to ERCOT for study. Refund of this financial security is subject to subsection (g),

 which provides that upon withdrawal, after payment of outstanding costs, only 20% of the

 remaining balance is refunded, with the remaining 80% retained by the interconnecting

 Transmission Service Provider ("TSP") and applied as an offset to rate base.

        For a project requesting 500 MW of peak demand, the intermediate-stage financial security

 totals $25 million. Under the proposed withdrawal framework, if a developer elects not to proceed,

 as much as $20 million of that amount may be forfeited—even where no interconnection facilities

 have been constructed, no stranded infrastructure costs have been incurred, and the developer's

 decision to withdraw is driven entirely by the results of the interconnection study.

                                                  4
 B.      Policy Concerns with Pre-Study Non-Refundable Financial Exposure


       TCC respectfully submits that imposing substantial non-refundable financial exposure at

the intermediate agreement stage—prior to completion of the interconnection study—is

commercially unreasonable, inconsistent with the statutory objectives of PURA § 37.0561, and

creates outcomes that are neither fair nor efficient. Two circumstances illustrate the fundamental

problems with this structure.

       First, the large load customer does not know what level of grid service, if any, it will

receive. At the intermediate agreement stage, the developer has no information regarding whether

the system can deliver the requested MW on the requested timetable. The interconnection study

has not yet been initiated, let alone completed. The developer does not know how many other

projects are in the same area, how those projects interact with each other, or how system-wide

constraints will ultimately be resolved. Under the proposed batch study framework, the developer's

requested load ramp may be materially altered—reduced materially in magnitude as to become

commercially infeasible, deferred by years, or both—based on system-wide study results that are

entirely outside the developer's control.

       Requiring a developer to commit tens of millions of dollars in financial security, subject to

substantial forfeiture, before the developer has any basis on which to evaluate whether the

interconnection will be commercially viable is fundamentally inconsistent with sound regulatory

policy. The developer is being asked to accept a material, non-refundable financial risk in exchange

for the mere opportunity to learn what the system can support. In no other commercial or regulatory

context is a party required to forfeit substantial capital simply because a process that the party

cannot control yields a result that renders the investment uneconomic.



                                                 5
        The informational asymmetry is particularly acute under the batch study framework.

Unlike the prior individual study process, where a developer's request was evaluated on a project-

specific basis, the batch study evaluates all requests in a geographic area simultaneously. A

developer requesting 500 MW at a particular substation may have every reason to believe, based

on the substation's existing capacity and the developer's own analysis, that the request is

reasonable. But if four other developers have submitted requests for 500 MW at the same facility—

information the developer cannot access due to confidentiality requirements—the study results

may allocate only a fraction of the requested capacity to any one project. This outcome is entirely

unknowable at the time the intermediate agreement is executed and financial security is posted.

       Under these circumstances, the forfeiture of financial security is not a consequence of

speculative or non-viable behavior by the developer. It is a consequence of a system-wide planning

process that produces outcomes the developer could not have predicted. Penalizing developers for

the results of that process—rather than for their own conduct—does not advance any legitimate

policy objective and is commercially unreasonable. It sends the message that the Texas power grid

is closed to manufacturing and industrial development.

       Second, forfeiture at the intermediate stage represents a windfall to the

interconnecting utility. At the intermediate agreement stage, the utility's actual costs are limited

to the study fee and modest administrative expenses associated with processing the interconnection

request. The rule already requires the large load customer to pay a separate study fee under §

25.194(d)(9) to cover the costs of the interconnection study. The utility has not procured

equipment, has not begun construction, and has not incurred stranded infrastructure costs—indeed,

the rule itself prohibits the utility from procuring equipment or services until the large load

customer posts additional financial security for that purpose.


                                                 6
         Yet under the proposed structure, if the developer withdraws following an unfavorable

study result, the utility retains up to 80% of the financial security after applying the security to any

outstanding costs—which at the intermediate stage are likely to be minimal or nonexistent. The

forfeited amount bears no relationship to any cost incurred by the utility or any risk to the system.

It is, in substance, a windfall—a transfer of wealth from the developer to the utility (and ultimately

to the utility's rate base) that is not grounded in cost causation, actual system impact, or identifiable

harm.

        This outcome is particularly problematic because the forfeited funds are directed to be

applied as an offset to the TSP's rate base, benefiting the utility's existing ratepayers at the expense

of a developer that received nothing in return. The developer paid for the privilege of entering a

study queue, received study results that rendered its project uneconomic, withdrew in a

commercially rational manner, and lost tens of millions of dollars—none of which were

attributable to costs the utility actually incurred. This is not cost recovery; it is an unearned

financial benefit to the utility that is disconnected from any statutory purpose.

C.      Recommended Revisions


     To address these concerns, TCC recommends that the Commission revise the financial security

framework at the intermediate agreement stage as follows:

     1. Financial security posted at the intermediate agreement stage should remain substantially
        refundable until completion of the interconnection study and execution of the
        interconnection agreement. Non-refundable exposure at this stage should be limited to
        amounts necessary to cover actual costs incurred by the interconnecting utility, including
        study fees, administrative costs, and any non-cancellable procurement undertaken at the
        developer's request.

     2. If a large load customer withdraws following completion of the interconnection study—
        including where the study results materially differ from the developer's original request—
        the financial security should be refunded in full, less any amounts attributable to actual,
        documented costs incurred by the utility.

                                                   7
        3. The transition from refundable to non-refundable financial commitments should occur at
          the interconnection agreement stage, after the developer has received the study results and
          has sufficient information to make an informed investment decision. At that point, the
          developer has accepted the study outcome and elected to proceed, and the imposition of
          non-refundable financial obligations is appropriately calibrated to the developer's
          voluntary commitment.

       This approach preserves the screening function of the intermediate-stage financial security

  requirement—demonstrating that the developer has the financial capacity and seriousness of

  purpose to participate in the interconnection process—while ensuring that forfeiture is tied to

  actual costs and developer-controlled decisions rather than to system-wide planning outcomes that

 are beyond the developer's control.

III.      THE 80% NON-REFUNDABLE FORFEITURE STRUCTURE AT THE
          INTERCONNECTION AGREEMENT STAGE

 A.       The Proposed Structure


          Under proposed § 25.194(g), when a large load customer withdraws all or a portion of its

 requested or contracted peak demand, the interconnecting utility must first apply the customer's

 financial security to any outstanding amounts owed, then refund 20% of the remaining balance,

 and transfer the remaining 80% to the interconnecting TSP for application as an offset to the TSP's

 rate base. An identical 80/20 forfeiture structure applies under proposed § 25.194(h) for non-

 utilized capacity.

          In addition, under proposed § 25.194(f)(7), the large load customer must pay a non-

 refundable interconnection fee of $50,000 per MW of contracted peak demand at the

 interconnection agreement stage. This fee is drawn from the financial security posted at the

 intermediate stage, with the balance of unused financial security then applied to cover financial

 security for significant equipment and services.


                                                    8
 B.     Policy Concerns with the 80% Non-Refundable Amount


       While TCC acknowledges that a degree of non-refundability at the interconnection

agreement stage is appropriate to ensure commitment and protect against stranded costs, the

proposed 80% forfeiture rate is excessive and disconnected from cost-causation principles.

       The utility should not recover more than its actual costs, and non-refundable

exposure should not exceed a reasonable margin above those costs. The proposed rule already

includes robust mechanisms to ensure that the interconnecting utility is made whole for its actual

costs: (i) the study fee covers the costs of the interconnection study; (ii) Contribution in Aid of

Construction ("CIAC") covers all direct interconnection costs; (iii) the financial security for

significant equipment and services covers the utility's procurement costs for long-lead equipment;

and (iv) the financial security for system upgrades covers the costs of necessary system

improvements. Upon withdrawal, the utility is entitled to draw down on the customer's financial

security to cover all outstanding amounts owed, including costs for equipment that cannot be

canceled, construction that cannot be stopped, and services that cannot be terminated.

       After the utility has been fully compensated for its actual, documented costs through these

mechanisms, the remaining financial security—by definition—represents amounts that exceed the

utility's cost exposure. Retaining 80% of that excess and applying it to rate base is not cost

recovery. It is a surplus above the utility's actual losses, and its retention serves no purpose

grounded in the statutory framework of PURA § 37.0561.

       TCC respectfully submits that a non-refundable amount exceeding 10% of the utility's

actual, documented costs associated with the interconnection is difficult to justify under cost-

causation principles. A 10% margin above actual costs incurred at the time of withdrawal provides

a reasonable buffer for administrative expenses, opportunity costs, and the inherent uncertainty in

                                                9
 cost estimation, while avoiding the creation of a windfall that transfers wealth from developers to

utilities and their ratepayers without a corresponding cost basis. Allowing the utility to retain 80%

of amounts that exceed its actual costs—potentially tens of millions of dollars—goes well beyond

any reasonable margin and converts financial security from a cost-recovery mechanism into a

punitive forfeiture that is untethered from the statutory purposes of interconnection standards.

        The forfeiture structure creates perverse incentives. An 80% forfeiture rate may

incentivize utilities to encourage or tolerate the withdrawal of large load customers, knowing that

the financial windfall from forfeiture will exceed the utility's actual costs and reduce their rate

base. Conversely, it may discourage developers from entering the interconnection process at all,

reducing the pipeline of projects that support economic development and grid reliability in Texas.

Neither outcome is consistent with the Commission's statutory mandate.

        The forfeiture structure undermines the Commission's ratemaking authority. By

mandating that 80% of forfeited financial security be applied as an offset to the TSP's rate base,

the proposed rule effectively predetermines the ratemaking treatment of these funds outside of a

PURA Chapter 36 proceeding. Whether and how forfeited amounts should be credited to rate base

is a question that involves the utility's overall revenue requirement, cost allocation, and the

interests of all customer classes—determinations that should be made in a ratemaking proceeding

with full evidentiary development, not in an interconnection standards rule.

C.      Recommended Revisions


     To address these concerns, TCC recommends that the Commission revise the withdrawal and

non-utilization provisions as follows:

     1. Upon withdrawal or non-utilization, the interconnecting utility should be entitled to apply
        the customer's financial security to all actual, documented costs incurred or committed in


                                                 10
          connection with the interconnection, including non-cancellable procurement, construction,
         and services.
      2. After the utility has been made whole for its actual costs, the utility may retain a non-
         refundable amount not to exceed 10% of the actual costs incurred at the time of withdrawal,
         to cover administrative and indirect costs associated with the interconnection process.
      3. The balance of the financial security remaining after application to actual costs and the
         10% fee on actual costs should be refunded to the large load customer.
      4. The treatment of any retained amounts for ratemaking purposes should not be
         predetermined within this rule but should instead be addressed in a future ratemaking
         proceeding under PURA Chapter 36, where the Commission can evaluate the appropriate
         treatment with the benefit of a full evidentiary record.

 This approach ensures that utilities are fully compensated for their actual costs, provides an

 appropriate margin above those costs to cover administrative and indirect expenses, and returns

 the balance to the developer. It is consistent with cost-causation principles, avoids creating an

 unearned financial benefit for utilities, and preserves the Commission's ratemaking authority under

 PURA Chapter 36.

IV.      FIVE-YEAR POST-ENERGIZATION SECURITY RETENTION PERIOD


 A.      The Proposed Structure


         Under proposed § 25.194(i), even after a large load customer successfully energizes and

 meets its phased energization milestones, the remaining balance of financial security is not fully

 refunded until the customer sustains operations for five years at its contracted peak demand. The

 rule provides that only 20% of the remaining balance is refunded at energization—ratably as the

 customer meets phased milestones—with the full remaining balance returned only upon

 completion of the five-year sustained operations period.

 B.       Policy Concerns with the Five-Year Retention Period


         TCC recognizes the policy rationale underlying this provision. The concern is that if large

 load customers were to cease or substantially reduce operations shortly after energization,

                                                 11
 ratepayers could be left bearing increased transmission costs associated with system upgrades built

to serve those loads. Financial security retention provides assurance that the customer will

maintain operations for a sufficient period to allow the utility to amortize interconnection-related

investments through rates.

        However, the five-year post-energization retention period is excessive and inconsistent

with current utility practice. Today, utility treatment of post-energization security varies across

ERCOT, but in practice, many utilities refund financial security upon initial energization or upon

reaching a required level of operation within a specified time period of energization in order to

ensure that the transmission built to serve the project is utilized and used and useful. The proposed

five-year retention goes well beyond existing practice and imposes an extended collateral

obligation that is not proportionate to the utility’s actual post-energization risk exposure.

C.      Recommended Revisions


     Rather than imposing a blanket five-year security retention period on all large load customers,

TCC respectfully recommends that the Commission adopt an alternative approach that more

closely ties the post-energization financial framework to cost causation. Specifically, TCC

recommends the following revisions:

1. Financial security should be refunded to the large load customer once the customer reaches
   and sustains the contracted level of operation, consistent with the approach historically
   followed by most interconnecting utilities in ERCOT. A customer that has energized and is
   operating at its contracted peak demand has demonstrated the commitment and operational
   viability that the financial security was intended to assure.
2. To address the Commission’s legitimate concern regarding ratepayer exposure in the event of
   post-energization load departure, the Commission should consider establishing a minimum
   demand charge applicable to large load customers. This charge would be reflected in the
   customer’s standard rate schedule and would apply for a defined period—such as five years
   from the date of initial energization—functioning as a demand ratchet that provides revenue
   assurance to the utility during the critical post-energization period. This structure could be
   addressed in a rate case, rather than this rule.


                                                 12
  3. A demand ratchet mechanism is preferable to prolonged security retention because it ties the
    customer’s ongoing financial obligation to actual service consumption and cost causation,
    rather than requiring the customer to maintain a separate collateral deposit for an extended
    period. It also will still providing meaningful protection against the scenario in which a large
    load departure shifts transmission costs to other customer classes or customers within the class
    due to failure to meet the requested level of operation over a sustained period.
 4. The demand ratchet could be designed to phase out over the five-year period, declining ratably
    as the utility’s investment is amortized through rates, thereby balancing ratepayer protection
    with the customer’s legitimate interest in not bearing indefinite financial obligations beyond
    the point at which the interconnection investment has been substantially recovered.
      This approach achieves the same policy objective as the five-year retention—ensuring that

 utilities can recover their transmission investment over a reasonable period—while more closely

 aligning the mechanism with cost-causation principles and avoiding the imposition of extended

 collateral requirements that are not calibrated to actual post-energization risk.

V.       TIMING OF FINANCIAL SECURITY POSTING AND TIERED SECURITY
         AMOUNTS

 A.      The Per-MW Amount Should Be Tiered to Reflect Project Maturity


         TCC respectfully submits that the proposed rule’s requirement of $50,000 per MW at both

 the intermediate agreement stage and the interconnection agreement stage fails to account for the

 significant difference in project maturity and information available to the developer at each stage.

 As discussed in Section II of these comments, the intermediate agreement stage is characterized

 by maximum informational uncertainty: the interconnection study has not yet commenced, the

 large load customer does not know what level of service will ultimately be deliverable, and the

 customer has no basis on which to assess the commercial viability of its proposed interconnection.

 Requiring $50,000 per MW at this stage — the same rate that applies at the interconnection

 agreement stage under proposed § 25.194(f)(7), where the customer has the benefit of completed

 study results — imposes financial exposure that is disproportionate to the customer’s available

 information and the utility’s actual risk.

                                                  13
          TCC recommends that the Commission adopt a tiered financial security structure that

reflects the progression of the interconnection process. Under this approach, the per-MW financial

security requirement at the intermediate agreement stage would be reduced to $25,000 per MW,

with the full $50,000 per MW applying as a step-up at the interconnection agreement stage. This

structure would still require a meaningful financial commitment at the intermediate stage — $12.5

million for a 500 MW project — while appropriately reflecting the pre-study nature of the

commitment and the limited information available to the developer. The step-up to $50,000 per

MW at the interconnection agreement stage would occur only after the developer has received and

had the opportunity to evaluate the interconnection study results, at which point a higher level of

financial commitment is justified by the developer’s informed, voluntary decision to proceed.

         This tiered approach preserves the screening function of the financial security requirement

while ensuring that the magnitude of the commitment is proportionate to the stage of the

interconnection process. A developer posting $25,000 per MW in financial security has

demonstrated substantial financial capacity and seriousness of purpose; the incremental step-up to

$50,000 per MW at the interconnection agreement stage appropriately reflects the developer’s

informed acceptance of the study outcome and decision to commit to the project on a long-term

basis.

B.       The Window for Posting Financial Security Should Provide 90 Days from Execution
         of the Interconnection Agreement

         Under the proposed rule, financial security is due at the time the intermediate agreement is

executed. This effectively requires the large load customer to arrange and post security

simultaneously with — or immediately upon — execution of the agreement, with no separate

window for negotiating the necessary extension agreements with the utility, arranging letters of

credit or other financing instruments, and completing internal corporate approvals.

                                                 14
        Given the proposed step up in security at the Interconnection Agreement phase, TCC

recommends that the proposed rule be revised to require the large load customer to execute the

Interconnection Agreement within 30 days, with financial security to be posted no later than 90

days after execution. This structure allows the customer to demonstrate its commitment to the

process promptly by executing the full interconnection agreement, while providing sufficient time

thereafter to arrange the substantial financial instruments required under the rule.

       The practical necessity of this extended posting window cannot be overstated. In TCC’s

experience, utilities are not typically equipped to move with the speed that a simultaneous or 30-

day posting requirement demands. Utilities often take 15-30 days or even longer simply to respond

to customer inquiries regarding extension agreements. Moreover, there is no standard form of

extension agreement across the utilities operating in ERCOT, and utilities frequently include

special provisions that are not reflected in existing tariffs and that ultimately require negotiation.

       For a 500 MW project at the $50,000 per MW rate at the interconnection agreement phase,

the customer must arrange $25 million in financial security (i.e., an incremental $12.5 million) —

a process that necessarily involves negotiation of letter of credit terms with financial institutions,

internal corporate and board-level approvals, and coordination with legal counsel. The customer

must also address any unique special provisions that are not standard in the utility agreement.

Thirty days is simply not a feasible period in which to accomplish all of these steps, particularly

when the utility itself may require weeks to respond to initial inquiries.

       By comparison, Georgia Power’s transmission service process provides customers 90 days

to arrange financing after the MW commitment number is issued — a reasonable benchmark that

reflects the practical realities of arranging large-scale financial instruments in the utility context.

The Commission should adopt a comparable approach. A 90-day posting window, following a 30-


                                                  15
  day execution period, provides a firm and enforceable timeline that demonstrates project

 seriousness while accommodating the legitimate practical constraints that large load customers

 face in arranging financial security of this magnitude.

VI.     CONCLUSION


        TCC supports the Commission's efforts to establish a structured and transparent framework

 for large load interconnection in ERCOT. The transition to a batch study process and the

 codification of interconnection standards under PURA § 37.0561 represent important steps toward

 managing the growth of large load demand while maintaining system reliability.

        However, the financial security and refund provisions of the proposed rule, as currently

 structured, impose financial consequences that are disproportionate to actual system costs,

 disconnected from cost-causation principles, and ultimately counterproductive to the statutory

 objective of supporting business development in Texas. The proposed security framework also

 creates barriers to entry that disproportionately burden smaller and mid-market developers,

 concentrating market participation among the most heavily capitalized firms. Developers should

 not be required to forfeit tens of millions of dollars based on system-wide study outcomes they

 cannot control, and utilities should not be permitted to retain amounts that vastly exceed their

 actual costs.

        TCC respectfully requests that the Commission revise the proposed rule to (i) ensure that

 financial security at the intermediate agreement stage remains substantially refundable until the

 developer has sufficient information to make an informed investment decision; (ii) limit non-

 refundable exposure upon withdrawal or non-utilization to the utility's actual costs plus a

 reasonable administrative margin not to exceed 10% of actual costs incurred at the time of

 withdrawal; (iii) replace the five-year post-energization security retention period with a refund

                                                 16
 upon sustained operation at contracted levels, supplemented by a minimum demand charge for

large loads that functions as a phased demand ratchet; (iv) adopt a tiered financial security structure

of $25,000 per MW at the intermediate agreement stage stepping up to $50,000 per MW at the

interconnection agreement stage, and extend the posting window to 90 days from execution of the

interconnection agreement; and (v) support the separation of rule-related interconnection

requirements from PGRR145, as recommended in Commission Staff’s April 13, 2026

memorandum. These targeted refinements preserve the core structure and objectives of the

proposed rule while ensuring that financial requirements are calibrated to actual risk, grounded in

cost causation, and consistent with PURA § 37.0561.

       TCC appreciates the Commission's consideration of these comments and looks forward to

continued engagement in this proceeding.



                                                       Respectfully submitted,

                                                       /s/ Scott Krikorian

                                                       Scott Krikorian
                                                       Senior Managing Director
                                                       Trammell Crow Company
                                                       2100 McKinney Avenue, Suite 800
                                                       Dallas, Texas 75201
                                                       214-863-3500




                                                  17
                                       PROJECT NO. 58481


RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                          §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                       §
STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                   §                     OF TEXAS



                TRAMMELL CROW COMPANY’S EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

•   Revise Intermediate-Stage Refundability. Financial security posted at the intermediate

    agreement stage ($50,000/MW) should remain substantially refundable until completion of the

    interconnection study. Non-refundable exposure at this stage should be limited to actual costs

    incurred by the utility. At the intermediate stage, the large load customer does not know if the

    system can deliver the requested MW on the requested timetable. Forfeiture driven by system-

    wide study outcomes, rather than developer conduct, is inconsistent with PURA § 37.0561.

•   Eliminate Windfall to Utilities at the Intermediate Stage. Forfeiture of financial security at

    the intermediate stage, where the utility has incurred minimal costs, represents an unearned

    financial benefit to the utility that is disconnected from cost causation, actual system impact,

    or identifiable harm. Forfeited amounts should not exceed actual, documented costs.

•   Reduce Non-Refundable Exposure Upon Withdrawal at the Interconnection Agreement

    Stage. The 80% forfeiture of remaining financial security upon withdrawal or non-utilization

    is excessive and exceeds any reasonable measure of the utility's actual cost exposure. After the

    utility has been made whole for actual costs through draw-down on financial security, CIAC,

    and study fees, the remaining balance represents amounts in excess of the utility's losses.

    Utilities should not recover more than 10% above actual, documented costs.




                                                18
 •   Preserve Commission Ratemaking Authority. The proposed rule should not predetermine

    that forfeited financial security be applied as an offset to the TSP's rate base. The ratemaking

    treatment of retained funds should be addressed in a PURA Chapter 36 proceeding.

•   Align Financial Consequences with Cost Causation and Developer Conduct. Forfeiture

    should be triggered by actual cost incurrence and developer-controlled actions, not by system-

    wide study outcomes or feasibility determinations outside the developer's control. Financial

    security should function as a cost-recovery and risk-mitigation tool, not as a punitive

    mechanism or system-wide funding source.

•   Replace Five-Year Post-Energization Security Retention with a Minimum Demand

    Charge in a Rate Case. The proposed five-year retention period for financial security

    following energization exceeds current utility practice in Texas and is not proportionate to

    post-energization risk. Financial security should be refunded once the customer reaches and

    sustains the contracted level of operation. The Commission should instead consider a minimum

    demand charge for large loads, applied for a defined period as a demand ratchet that phases

    out over time, to achieve the same ratepayer protection objective through a mechanism more

    closely tied to cost causation.

•   Adopt Tiered Financial Security Amounts and Extend the Posting Window. The proposed

    rule requires $50,000 per MW at both the intermediate and interconnection agreement stages,

II.     NON-REFUNDABILITY OF FINANCIAL SECURITY AT THE
        INTERMEDIATE AGREEMENT STAGE

 A.     The Proposed Structure


        Under proposed § 25.194(d)(10), a large load customer must post financial security in the

 amount of $50,000 per MW of requested peak demand at the time the intermediate agreement is

 executed. This financial security is posted before the large load customer's interconnection request

 is submitted to ERCOT for study. Refund of this financial security is subject to subsection (g),

 which provides that upon withdrawal, after payment of outstanding costs, only 20% of the

 remaining balance is refunded, with the remaining 80% retained by the interconnecting

 Transmission Service Provider ("TSP") and applied as an offset to rate base.

        For a project requesting 500 MW of peak demand, the intermediate-stage financial security

 totals $25 million. Under the proposed withdrawal framework, if a developer elects not to proceed,

 as much as $20 million ofthat amount may be forfeited-even where no interconnection facilities

 have been constructed, no stranded infrastructure costs have been incurred, and the developer's

 decision to withdraw is driven entirely by the results ofthe interconnection study.

                                                  4
 B.      Policy Concerns with Pre-Study Non-Refundable Financial Exposure


       TCC respectfully submits that imposing substantial non-refundable financial exposure at

the intermediate agreement stage--prior to completion of the interconnection study-is

commercially unreasonable, inconsistent with the statutory objectives of PURA § 37.0561, and

creates outcomes that are neither fair nor efficient. Two circumstances illustrate the fundamental

problems with this structure.

       First, the large load customer does not know what level of grid service, if any, it will

receive. At the intermediate agreement stage, the developer has no information regarding whether

the system can deliver the requested MW on the requested timetable. The interconnection study

has not yet been initiated, let alone completed. The developer does not know how many other

proj ects are in the same area, how those proj ects interact with each other, or how system-wide

constraints will ultimately be resolved. Under the proposed batch study framework, the developer's

requested load ramp may be materially altered-reduced materially in magnitude as to become

commercially infeasible, deferred by years, or both-based on system-wide study results that are

entirely outside the developer's control.

       Requiring a developer to commit tens of millions of dollars in financial security, subj ect to

substantial forfeiture, before the developer has any basis on which to evaluate whether the

interconnection will be commercially viable is fundamentally inconsistent with sound regulatory

policy. The developer is being asked to accept a material, non-refundable financial risk in exchange

for the mere opportunity to learn what the system can support. In no other commercial or regulatory

context is a party required to forfeit substantial capital simply because a process that the party

cannot control yields a result that renders the investment uneconomic.



                                                 5
        The informational asymmetry is particularly acute under the batch study framework.

Unlike the prior individual study process, where a developer's request was evaluated on a project-

specific basis, the batch study evaluates all requests in a geographic area simultaneously. A

developer requesting 500 MW at a particular substation may have every reason to believe, based

on the substation's existing capacity and the developer's own analysis, that the request is

reasonable. But if four other developers have submitted requests for 500 MW at the same facility-

information the developer cannot access due to confidentiality requirements-the study results

may allocate only a fraction of the requested capacity to any one project. This outcome is entirely

unknowable at the time the intermediate agreement is executed and financial security is posted.

       Under these circumstances, the forfeiture of financial security is not a consequence of

speculative or non-viable behavior by the developer. It is a consequence of a system-wide planning

process that produces outcomes the developer could not have predicted. Penalizing developers for

the results of that process-rather than for their own conduct-does not advance any legitimate

policy objective and is commercially unreasonable. It sends the message that the Texas power grid

is closed to manufacturing and industrial development.

       Second, forfeiture at the intermediate stage represents a windfall to the

interconnecting utility. At the intermediate agreement stage, the utility's actual costs are limited

to the study fee and modest administrative expenses associated with processing the interconnection

request. The rule already requires the large load customer to pay a separate study fee under §

25.194(d)(9) to cover the costs of the interconnection study. The utility has not procured

equipment, has not begun construction, and has not incurred stranded infrastructure costs-indeed,

the rule itself prohibits the utility from procuring equipment or services until the large load

customer posts additional financial security for that purpose.


                                                 6
          Yet under the proposed structure, if the developer withdraws following an unfavorable

study result, the utility retains up to 80% of the financial security after applying the security to any

outstanding costs-which at the intermediate stage are likely to be minimal or nonexistent. The

forfeited amount bears no relationship to any cost incurred by the utility or any risk to the system.

It is, in substance, a windfall-a transfer of wealth from the developer to the utility (and ultimately

to the utility's rate base) that is not grounded in cost causation, actual system impact, or identifiable

harrn.

         This outcome is particularly problematic because the forfeited funds are directed to be

applied as an offset to the TSP's rate base, benefiting the utility's existing ratepayers at the expense

of a developer that received nothing in return. The developer paid for the privilege of entering a

study queue, received study results that rendered its proj ect uneconomic, withdrew in a

commercially rational manner, and lost tens of millions of dollars-none of which were

attributable to costs the utility actually incurred. This is not cost recovery; it is an unearned

financial benefit to the utility that is disconnected from any statutory purpose.

C.       Recommended Revisions


     To address these concerns, TCC recommends that the Commission revise the financial security

framework at the intermediate agreement stage as follows:

     1. Financial security posted at the intermediate agreement stage should remain substantially
         refundable until completion of the interconnection study and execution of the
         interconnection agreement. Non-refundable exposure at this stage should be limited to
         amounts necessary to cover actual costs incurred by the interconnecting utility, including
         study fees, administrative costs, and any non-cancellable procurement undertaken at the
         developer's request.

     2. If a large load customer withdraws following completion of the interconnection study-
         including where the study results materially differ from the developer's original request-
         the financial security should be refunded in full, less any amounts attributable to actual,
         documented costs incurred by the utility.

                                                   7
        3. The transition from refundable to non-refundable financial commitments should occur at
          the interconnection agreement stage, after the developer has received the study results and
          has sufficient information to make an informed investment decision. At that point, the
          developer has accepted the study outcome and elected to proceed, and the imposition of
          non-refundable financial obligations is appropriately calibrated to the developer's
          voluntary commitment.

       This approach preserves the screening function of the intermediate-stage financial security

  requirement-demonstrating that the developer has the financial capacity and seriousness of

  purpose to participate in the interconnection process-while ensuring that forfeiture is tied to

  actual costs and developer-controlled decisions rather than to system-wide planning outcomes that

  are beyond the developer's control.

III.      THE 80% NON-REFUNDABLE FORFEITURE STRUCTURE AT THE
          INTERCONNECTION AGREEMENT STAGE

  A.      The Proposed Structure


          Under proposed § 25.194(g), when a large load customer withdraws all or a portion of its

  requested or contracted peak demand, the interconnecting utility must first apply the customer's

  financial security to any outstanding amounts owed, then refund 20% of the remaining balance,

  and transfer the remaining 80% to the interconnecting TSP for application as an offset to the TSP's

  rate base. An identical 80/20 forfeiture structure applies under proposed § 25. 194(h) for non-

  utilized capacity.

          In addition, under proposed § 25.194(f)(7), the large load customer must pay a non-

  refundable interconnection fee of $50,000 per MW of contracted peak demand at the

  interconnection agreement stage. This fee is drawn from the financial security posted at the

  intermediate stage, with the balance of unused financial security then applied to cover financial

  security for significant equipment and services.


                                                     8
 B.     Policy Concerns with the 80% Non-Refundable Amount


       While TCC acknowledges that a degree of non-refundability at the interconnection

agreement stage is appropriate to ensure commitment and protect against stranded costs, the

proposed 80% forfeiture rate is excessive and disconnected from cost-causation principles.

       The utility should not recover more than its actual costs, and non-refundable

exposure should not exceed a reasonable margin above those costs. The proposed rule already

includes robust mechanisms to ensure that the interconnecting utility is made whole for its actual

costs: (i) the study fee covers the costs of the interconnection study; (ii) Contribution in Aid of

Construction ("CIAC") covers all direct interconnection costs; (iii) the financial security for

significant equipment and services covers the utility's procurement costs for long-lead equipment;

and (iv) the financial security for system upgrades covers the costs of necessary system

improvements. Upon withdrawal, the utility is entitled to draw down on the customer's financial

security to cover all outstanding amounts owed, including costs for equipment that cannot be

canceled, construction that cannot be stopped, and services that cannot be terminated.

       After the utility has been fully compensated for its actual, documented costs through these

mechanisms, the remaining financial security-by definition-represents amounts that exceed the

utility's cost exposure. Retaining 80% of that excess and applying it to rate base is not cost

recovery. It is a surplus above the utility's actual losses, and its retention serves no purpose

grounded in the statutory framework of PURA § 37.0561.

       TCC respectfully submits that a non-refundable amount exceeding 10% of the utility's

actual, documented costs associated with the interconnection is difficult to justify under cost-

causation principles. A 10% margin above actual costs incurred at the time of withdrawal provides

a reasonable buffer for administrative expenses, opportunity costs, and the inherent uncertainty in

                                                9
 cost estimation, while avoiding the creation of a windfall that transfers wealth from developers to

utilities and their ratepayers without a corresponding cost basis. Allowing the utility to retain 80%

of amounts that exceed its actual costs-potentially tens of millions of dollars-goes well beyond

any reasonable margin and converts financial security from a cost-recovery mechanism into a

punitive forfeiture that is untethered from the statutory purposes of interconnection standards.

        The forfeiture structure creates perverse incentives. An 80% forfeiture rate may

incentivize utilities to encourage or tolerate the withdrawal of large load customers, knowing that

the financial windfall from forfeiture will exceed the utility's actual costs and reduce their rate

base. Conversely, it may discourage developers from entering the interconnection process at all,

reducing the pipeline of projects that support economic development and grid reliability in Texas.

Neither outcome is consistent with the Commission's statutory mandate.

        The forfeiture structure undermines the Commission's ratemaking authority. By

mandating that 80% of forfeited financial security be applied as an offset to the TSP's rate base,

the proposed rule effectively predetermines the ratemaking treatment of these funds outside of a

PURA Chapter 36 proceeding. Whether and how forfeited amounts should be credited to rate base

is a question that involves the utility's overall revenue requirement, cost allocation, and the

interests of all customer classes-determinations that should be made in a ratemaking proceeding

with full evidentiary development, not in an interconnection standards rule.

C.      Recommended Revisions


     To address these concerns, TCC recommends that the Commission revise the withdrawal and

non-utilization provisions as follows:

     1. Upon withdrawal or non-utilization, the interconnecting utility should be entitled to apply
        the customer's financial security to all actual, documented costs incurred or committed in


                                                 10
          connection with the interconnection, including non-cancellable procurement, construction,
         and services.
      2. After the utility has been made whole for its actual costs, the utility may retain a non-
         refundable amount not to exceed 10% ofthe actual costs incurred at the time ofwithdrawal,
         to cover administrative and indirect costs associated with the interconnection process.
      3. The balance of the financial security remaining after application to actual costs and the
         10% fee on actual costs should be refunded to the large load customer.
      4. The treatment of any retained amounts for ratemaking purposes should not be
         predetermined within this rule but should instead be addressed in a future ratemaking
         proceeding under PURA Chapter 36, where the Commission can evaluate the appropriate
         treatment with the benefit of a full evidentiary record.

 This approach ensures that utilities are fully compensated for their actual costs, provides an

 appropriate margin above those costs to cover administrative and indirect expenses, and returns

 the balance to the developer. It is consistent with cost-causation principles, avoids creating an

 unearned financial benefit for utilities, and preserves the Commission's ratemaking authority under

 PURA Chapter 36.

IV.      FIVE-YEAR POST-ENERGIZATION SECURITY RETENTION PERIOD


 A.      The Proposed Structure


         Under proposed § 25.194(i), even after a large load customer successfully energizes and

 meets its phased energization milestones, the remaining balance of financial security is not fully

 refunded until the customer sustains operations for five years at its contracted peak demand. The

 rule provides that only 20% of the remaining balance is refunded at energization-ratably as the

 customer meets phased milestones-with the full remaining balance returned only upon

 completion of the five-year sustained operations period.

 B.       Policy Concerns with the Five-Year Retention Period


         TCC recognizes the policy rationale underlying this provision. The concern is that if large

 load customers were to cease or substantially reduce operations shortly after energization,

                                                 11
 ratepayers could be left bearing increased transmission costs associated with system upgrades built

to serve those loads. Financial security retention provides assurance that the customer will

maintain operations for a sufficient period to allow the utility to amortize interconnection-related

investments through rates.

        However, the five-year post-energization retention period is excessive and inconsistent

with current utility practice. Today, utility treatment of post-energization security varies across

ERCOT, but in practice, many utilities refund financial security upon initial energization or upon

reaching a required level of operation within a specified time period of energization in order to

ensure that the transmission built to serve the project is utilized and used and useful. The proposed

five-year retention goes well beyond existing practice and imposes an extended collateral

obligation that is not proportionate to the utility' s actual post-energization risk exposure.

C.      Recommended Revisions


     Rather than imposing a blanket five-year security retention period on alllarge load customers,

TCC respectfully recommends that the Commission adopt an alternative approach that more

closely ties the post-energization financial framework to cost causation. Specifically, TCC

recommends the following revisions:

1. Financial security should be refunded to the large load customer once the customer reaches
   and sustains the contracted level of operation, consistent with the approach historically
   followed by most interconnecting utilities in ERCOT. A customer that has energized and is
   operating at its contracted peak demand has demonstrated the commitment and operational
   viability that the financial security was intended to assure.
2. To address the Commission' s legitimate concern regarding ratepayer exposure in the event of
   post-energization load departure, the Commission should consider establishing a minimum
     demand charge applicable to large load customers. This charge would be reflected in the
     customer' s standard rate schedule and would apply for a defined period-such as five years
     from the date of initial energization-functioning as a demand ratchet that provides revenue
     assurance to the utility during the critical post-energization period. This structure could be
     addressed in a rate case, rather than this rule.


                                                    12
  3. A demand ratchet mechanism is preferable to prolonged security retention because it ties the
    customer' s ongoing financial obligation to actual service consumption and cost causation,
    rather than requiring the customer to maintain a separate collateral deposit for an extended
    period. It also will still providing meaningful protection against the scenario in which a large
    load departure shifts transmission costs to other customer classes or customers within the class
    due to failure to meet the requested level of operation over a sustained period.
 4. The demand ratchet could be designed to phase out over the five-year period, declining ratably
    as the utility' s investment is amortized through rates, thereby balancing ratepayer protection
    with the customer' s legitimate interest in not bearing indefinite financial obligations beyond
    the point at which the interconnection investment has been substantially recovered.

      This approach achieves the same policy objective as the five-year retention-ensuring that

 utilities can recover their transmission investment over a reasonable period-while more closely

 aligning the mechanism with cost-causation principles and avoiding the imposition of extended

 collateral requirements that are not calibrated to actual post-energization risk.

V.       TIMING OF FINANCIAL SECURITY POSTING AND TIERED SECURITY
         AMOUNTS

 A.      The Per-MW Amount Should Be Tiered to Reflect Project Maturity


         TCC respectfully submits that the proposed rule's requirement of $50,000 per MW at both

 the intermediate agreement stage and the interconnection agreement stage fails to account for the

 significant difference in proj ect maturity and information available to the developer at each stage.

 As discussed in Section II of these comments, the intermediate agreement stage is characterized

 by maximum informational uncertainty: the interconnection study has not yet commenced, the

 large load customer does not know what level of service will ultimately be deliverable, and the

 customer has no basis on which to assess the commercial viability of its proposed interconnection.

 Requiring $50,000 per MW at this stage - the same rate that applies at the interconnection

 agreement stage under proposed § 25.194(f)(7), where the customer has the benefit of completed

 study results - imposes financial exposure that is disproportionate to the customer's available

 information and the utility' s actual risk.

                                                   13
          TCC recommends that the Commission adopt a tiered financial security structure that

reflects the progression of the interconnection process. Under this approach, the per-MW financial

security requirement at the intermediate agreement stage would be reduced to $25,000 per MW,

with the full $50,000 per MW applying as a step-up at the interconnection agreement stage. This

structure would still require a meaningful financial commitment at the intermediate stage - $12.5

million for a 500 MW project - while appropriately reflecting the pre-study nature of the

commitment and the limited information available to the developer. The step-up to $50,000 per

MW at the interconnection agreement stage would occur only after the developer has received and

had the opportunity to evaluate the interconnection study results, at which point a higher level of

financial commitment is justified by the developer's informed, voluntary decision to proceed.

         This tiered approach preserves the screening function ofthe financial security requirement

while ensuring that the magnitude of the commitment is proportionate to the stage of the

interconnection process. A developer posting $25,000 per MW in financial security has

demonstrated substantial financial capacity and seriousness of purpose; the incremental step-up to

$50,000 per MW at the interconnection agreement stage appropriately reflects the developer's

informed acceptance of the study outcome and decision to commit to the proj ect on a long-term

basis.

B.       The Window for Posting Financial Security Should Provide 90 Days from Execution
         of the Interconnection Agreement

         Under the proposed rule, financial security is due at the time the intermediate agreement is

executed. This effectively requires the large load customer to arrange and post security

simultaneously with - or immediately upon - execution of the agreement, with no separate

window for negotiating the necessary extension agreements with the utility, arranging letters of

credit or other financing instruments, and completing internal corporate approvals.

                                                  14
        Given the proposed step up in security at the Interconnection Agreement phase, TCC

recommends that the proposed rule be revised to require the large load customer to execute the

Interconnection Agreement within 30 days, with financial security to be posted no later than 90

days after execution. This structure allows the customer to demonstrate its commitment to the

process promptly by executing the full interconnection agreement, while providing sufficient time

thereafter to arrange the substantial financial instruments required under the rule.

       The practical necessity of this extended posting window cannot be overstated. In TCC's

experience, utilities are not typically equipped to move with the speed that a simultaneous or 30-

day posting requirement demands. Utilities often take 15-30 days or even longer simply to respond

to customer inquiries regarding extension agreements. Moreover, there is no standard form of

extension agreement across the utilities operating in ERCOT, and utilities frequently include

special provisions that are not reflected in existing tariffs and that ultimately require negotiation.

       For a 500 MW project at the $50,000 per MW rate at the interconnection agreement phase,

the customer must arrange $25 million in financial security (i.e., an incremental $12.5 million) -

a process that necessarily involves negotiation of letter of credit terms with financial institutions,

internal corporate and board-level approvals, and coordination with legal counsel. The customer

must also address any unique special provisions that are not standard in the utility agreement.

Thirty days is simply not a feasible period in which to accomplish all of these steps, particularly

when the utility itself may require weeks to respond to initial inquiries.

       By comparison, Georgia Power' s transmission service process provides customers 90 days

to arrange financing after the MW commitment number is issued - a reasonable benchmark that

reflects the practical realities of arranging large-scale financial instruments in the utility context.

The Commission should adopt a comparable approach. A 90-day posting window, following a 30-


                                                  15
  day execution period, provides a firm and enforceable timeline that demonstrates proj ect

 seriousness while accommodating the legitimate practical constraints that large load customers

 face in arranging financial security ofthis magnitude.

VI.      CONCLUSION


         TCC supports the Commission's efforts to establish a structured and transparent framework

 for large load interconnection in ERCOT. The transition to a batch study process and the

 codification of interconnection standards under PURA § 37.0561 represent important steps toward

 managing the growth of large load demand while maintaining system reliability.

         However, the financial security and refund provisions of the proposed rule, as currently

 structured, impose financial consequences that are disproportionate to actual system costs,

 disconnected from cost-causation principles, and ultimately counterproductive to the statutory

 objective of supporting business development in Texas. The proposed security framework also

 creates barriers to entry that disproportionately burden smaller and mid-market developers,

 concentrating market participation among the most heavily capitalized firms. Developers should

 not be required to forfeit tens of millions of dollars based on system-wide study outcomes they

 cannot control, and utilities should not be permitted to retain amounts that vastly exceed their

 actual costs.

         TCC respectfully requests that the Commission revise the proposed rule to (i) ensure that

 financial security at the intermediate agreement stage remains substantially refundable until the

 developer has sufficient information to make an informed investment decision; (ii) limit non-

 refundable exposure upon withdrawal or non-utilization to the utility's actual costs plus a

 reasonable administrative margin not to exceed 10% of actual costs incurred at the time of

 withdrawal; (iii) replace the five-year post-energization security retention period with a refund

                                                 16
 upon sustained operation at contracted levels, supplemented by a minimum demand charge for

large loads that functions as a phased demand ratchet; (iv) adopt a tiered financial security structure

of $25,000 per MW at the intermediate agreement stage stepping up to $50,000 per MW at the

interconnection agreement stage, and extend the posting window to 90 days from execution of the

interconnection agreement; and (v) support the separation of rule-related interconnection

requirements from PGRR145, as recommended in Commission Staff's April 13, 2026

memorandum. These targeted refinements preserve the core structure and objectives of the

proposed rule while ensuring that financial requirements are calibrated to actual risk, grounded in

cost causation, and consistent with PURA § 37.0561.

       TCC appreciates the Commission's consideration of these comments and looks forward to

continued engagement in this proceeding.

Align Financial Consequences with Cost Causation and Developer Conduct. Forfeiture

should be triggered by actual cost incurrence and developer-controlled actions, not by system-

wide study outcomes or feasibility determinations outside the developer's control. Financial

security should function as a cost-recovery and risk-mitigation tool, not as a punitive

mechanism or system-wide funding source.

Replace Five-Year Post-Energization Security Retention with a Minimum Demand

Charge in a Rate Case. The proposed five-year retention period for financial security

following energization exceeds current utility practice in Texas and is not proportionate to

post-energization risk. Financial security should be refunded once the customer reaches and

sustains the contracted level of operation. The Commission should instead consider a minimum

demand charge for large loads, applied for a defined period as a demand ratchet that phases

out over time, to achieve the same ratepayer protection obj ective through a mechanism more

closely tied to cost causation.

Adopt Tiered Financial Security Amounts and Extend the Posting Window. The proposed

rule requires $50,000 per MW at both the intermediate and interconnection agreement stages,

which fails to account for the significant difference in project maturity between these stages.

TCC recommends reducing the per-MW amount at the intermediate stage to $25,000, with a

step-up to $50,000 per MW at the interconnection agreement stage. In addition, the rule should

be revised to allow 30 days for execution of the interconnection agreement and 90 days from

execution for the customer to post financial security, reflecting the practical realities of

     arranging large-scale financing instruments and negotiating extension agreements and

•   Separation of Rule Requirements from PGRR145. TCC supports Staff' s memorandum

    recommending that rule-related interconnection requirements be stripped from PGRR145 and

    addressed exclusively through this rulemaking. Substantive interconnection standards and

    financial security requirements should be established through the Commission's notice-and-
